newsitem.title: USA: Response to U.S. move shows anti-Iraq pact weaker.
newsitem.headline: Response to U.S. move shows anti-Iraq pact weaker.

text.p: A lukewarm response from Washington's allies to U.S. cruise missile attacks on Iraq shows that time has eroded the coalition that drove Baghdad's forces out of Kuwait five years ago.
But U.S. leaders on Tuesday shrugged off the relative lack of support from foreign capitals for the strikes on Iraqi defence installations, saying it was America's job to lead the way.

Only Washington's closest friends -- Britain, Germany, Japan and Canada -- backed the strikes, which followed an Iraqi military push into the Western-protected Kurdish area of northern Iraq. Only Britain provided any logistical support.
France, which joins the United States and Britain in patrolling no-fly zones over northern and southern Iraq, voiced concern. Spain and Italy pointedly witheld approval.

In the Gulf, Kuwait said it "fully understood" the U.S. attack, but the initial reaction from Saudi Arabia and other U.S. allies was silence. Russia voiced outright hostility, calling the strikes unacceptable.

It was a far cry from the near unanimity during the 1991 Gulf War, when the United States led a coalition of more than 30 countries into battle to eject the Iraqi forces that had occupied Kuwait six months earlier.
U.S. President Bill Clinton appeared uncomfortable when asked at a White House news conference about the tepid world reaction but eventually said he was "satisfied" with the allied response.

Dismissing suggestions from some European officials that the forthcoming U.S. presidential election may have influenced his decision, Clinton said: "I think others feel that at this time there may be, for their own domestic purposes, some limits on how much they can do."

"We have historically ... taken the lead in matters like this. And I think this was our responsibility at this time," he said in remarks clearly aimed at criticism from Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole that he was showing weak leadership.

Defence Secretary William Perry said "we expect most of our allies to be supportive" but direct allied help had not been needed in the attack. Britain and France had promised to continue taking part in no-fly zone enforcement, which in the case of Operation Southern Watch over southern Iraq will now be extended north from the 32nd to the 33rd parallel, he said.
Despite the brave face put on by U.S. officials, differences between key players over how to deal with Iraq in the post-Gulf War era have been evident for some time.

At the United Nations, the United States has had to beat back attempts by France and Russia to ease sanctions imposed on Iraq after the Gulf War. U.S. officials have hinted that certain European countries care more for lucrative contracts with Iraq than for keeping Baghdad in check.

Recently, Washington has single-handedly delayed implementation of a U.N. plan to allow Iraq to export some oil and import food and other necessities. Although the United States finally approved the plan, this week's crisis was expected to further postpone it.

Compounding these differences has been uncertainty over the purpose of maintaining the Kurdish enclave in northern Iraq that has been protected by Western powers since major Iraqi repressions against the Kurds after the Gulf War.
The effect of the policy, never specifically endorsed by the United Nations, has been to create an autonomous Kurdish region that falls short of an independent state -- something no country supports.

Washington's NATO ally Turkey, which provides a base for the aircraft that enforce the no-fly zone over northern Iraq, had grown increasingly restive about the Kurdish area, seeing it as a safe haven for its own rebellious Kurds.

Even the United States supports the territorial integrity of Iraq and statements by some countries Tuesday reflected the feeling that there was nothing illegal about Iraq sending troops into the Kurdish area.

U.S. leaders on Tuesday played down the notion of defending the Kurds as the main reason for the missile strikes, stressing instead the aim of protecting the vulnerable oil-producing countries to the south of Iraq.
"We continue to see the greatest threat of (Iraqi President) Saddam Hussein to the region being in the south. And therefore, that's where we concentrated our attention," Perry told a news conference.
